q: What is a channel of distribution?
r: The path a product follows from producer to final customer
It may include wholesalers and retailers.
w: The list of media used to advertise a product to customers
That describes a promotional media plan.
The set of prices a company charges in different regions
That describes a pricing structure.
The group of employees who deliver products to a warehouse
That describes a team, not the path.

q: Which channel member buys goods in large quantities and resells them to retailers?
r: Wholesaler
It links producers with stores.
w: Consumer who buys goods for personal use at a store
Consumers are the final buyers.
Broker who earns a fee for arranging deals without owning goods
A broker does not take ownership.
Manufacturer who makes the goods in its own factories
That is the producer.

q: A maker of handmade soap sells directly to customers through its own website. What type of channel is this?
r: A direct channel
There are no middlemen.
w: An indirect channel that uses wholesalers and retailers
Middlemen are not involved here.
A dual channel that uses two different retail partners
Only one route is described.
A reverse channel that takes used products back
That moves products back to the maker.

q: What is an indirect channel?
r: A route that uses one or more middlemen between maker and buyer
Wholesalers and retailers are common examples.
w: A route where the maker sells straight to the final customer
That is a direct channel.
A route that is used only for products sold overseas
Indirect channels are not limited to exports.
A route that is used only for services and never for goods
Both goods and services can use them.

q: Why might a small snack maker use a distributor instead of selling to every store itself?
r: A distributor already reaches many stores and handles deliveries
It saves time and reaches more buyers.
w: A distributor always charges lower prices than the maker would
Distributors add their own fee.
A distributor removes the need to make a quality product
Quality still matters to buyers.
A distributor guarantees every store will stock the product
No stocking is guaranteed.

q: What is logistics?
r: Planning and managing the movement and storage of goods
It covers transport, warehousing and delivery.
w: Setting the selling price of goods based on competitor prices
That is a pricing decision.
Choosing which customers should receive coupons this season
That is a promotion decision.
Recording the money a business earns and spends each month
That is accounting.

q: What is a retailer?
r: A business that sells goods directly to final consumers
Stores and online shops are retailers.
w: A business that makes goods from raw materials in a plant
That is a manufacturer.
A business that sells goods only to other businesses in bulk
That is a wholesaler.
A business that moves goods but never sells them
That is a carrier.

q: A bike brand sells through its own stores, a big-box chain and its website. What is this approach called?
r: Multichannel distribution
It reaches customers through several routes.
w: Exclusive distribution through a single partner store
Several routes are used instead.
Intensive distribution that avoids any retailers at all
Retailers are being used.
Direct mail that avoids any stores
That is a promotion method.

q: A luxury watch maker lets only a few high-end jewelers sell its watches. Which distribution strategy is this?
r: Exclusive distribution
Few outlets keep an image of prestige.
w: Intensive distribution in every possible store
Many outlets are not used.
Selective distribution in a moderate number of stores
Very few outlets are used here.
Direct distribution through only its own app
Jewelers are being used.

q: A candy maker wants its product in nearly every grocery and convenience store. Which strategy fits?
r: Intensive distribution
It aims for wide availability.
w: Exclusive distribution through a single partner store
That limits availability.
Selective distribution in only a few specialty shops
That limits availability.
Direct distribution through its own factory shop
That limits availability.

q: What does inventory management do for a channel?
r: Keeps enough goods on hand without holding too much
It balances service and cost.
w: Sets the price the final customer pays at checkout
That is a pricing function.
Chooses the colors and design of a product package
That is a product decision.
Creates the advertisements that appear on television
That is a promotion function.

q: A store runs out of a popular item every weekend. What is the most likely channel problem?
r: Too little inventory is being ordered for peak demand
Demand outpaces supply on busy days.
w: The item is priced too low for any customer to want it
Low price would not cause stock-outs by itself.
The item has too many colors for customers to choose from
Variety does not cause stock-outs.
The item has no brand name that customers can recognize
A missing brand does not cause stock-outs.

q: What is a supply chain?
r: The network of businesses that move a product from raw materials to customer
It includes suppliers, makers and sellers.
w: The list of every price that a product has sold at
That is a price history.
The group of customers who buy a product regularly
That is a customer base.
The set of ads that a product appears in
That is a campaign.

q: A storm closes a key port and a retailer's shelves empty. Which approach best reduces this risk in the future?
r: Using more than one supplier and shipping route
Backups reduce dependence on one link.
w: Relying on one supplier to simplify the paperwork
That increases risk.
Ordering only at the last possible minute each time
That increases the risk of delays.
Ignoring delivery times when choosing suppliers
That increases the risk.

q: What is channel conflict?
r: A disagreement between members of a distribution channel
For example, a maker competes with its own retailers online.
w: A disagreement between two customers in a checkout line
That is not a channel matter.
A disagreement between a firm and its tax advisers
That is not a channel matter.
A disagreement between two employees on a work schedule
That is not a channel matter.

q: A maker starts selling online at lower prices than its retailers charge, and the retailers complain. What is this?
r: Channel conflict
Members of the channel are competing.
w: Price skimming used to launch a new product
The issue is competition among partners.
Market segmentation based on customer age
That is not what the retailers object to.
Brand extension into a related product line
That is not the issue.

q: What does a freight carrier do?
r: Transports goods from one location to another
Trucks, trains, ships and planes are carriers.
w: Creates the advertising for a product launch
That is an agency role.
Sets the final shelf price at a store location
That is a retailer decision.
Tests the quality of products before sale
That is quality control.

q: What is warehousing?
r: Storing goods until they are needed for sale or shipment
Warehouses hold stock in bulk.
w: Selling goods to final consumers in a shop
That is retailing.
Making goods from raw materials in a factory
That is manufacturing.
Promoting goods through public events
That is promotion.

q: What is a benefit of using drop shipping for a small online store?
r: The store does not need to hold inventory
The supplier ships directly to the customer.
w: The store controls packaging and shipping quality fully
The supplier handles shipping.
The store earns the full retail price as profit
The supplier takes its share.
The store never needs to deal with returns
Returns still need handling.

q: What is a reverse channel?
r: A route that returns used or defective products to the maker
It supports recycling and returns.
w: A route that delivers new products to customers faster
That is a regular channel.
A route that is used only for foreign sales
That is not the meaning.
A route that removes retailers from the channel
That is disintermediation.

q: What is order fulfillment?
r: The steps from receiving an order to delivering it to the customer
It includes picking, packing and shipping.
w: The steps for designing a new product line
That is product development.
The steps for hiring new staff for a store
That is human resources.
The steps for filing a company's yearly taxes
That is accounting.

q: Which measure best shows whether order fulfillment is working well?
r: The percent of orders delivered correctly and on time
It tracks service reliability.
w: The number of colors in the company's logo
That is a design detail.
The number of followers on the company's account
That is a promotion measure.
The length of the company's mission statement
That is not a performance measure.

q: Why do many companies use retailers rather than only selling directly?
r: Retailers give customers convenient places to see and buy products
They add reach and convenience.
w: Retailers pay the manufacturer's tax bills each year
That is not their role.
Retailers design the products that the maker will sell
That is the maker's role.
Retailers remove all competition from the market
That is not their role.

q: What is marketing research?
r: Gathering and studying information about customers and markets
It guides marketing decisions.
w: Setting prices based on a competitor's latest sale
That is a pricing tactic.
Delivering products to customers on a set schedule
That is distribution.
Training employees to greet customers politely
That is staff training.

q: What is primary research?
r: Information a business collects itself for a specific purpose
Surveys and interviews are examples.
w: Information that was collected earlier by someone else
That is secondary research.
Information that is purchased from a data broker only
That is a form of secondary data.
Information that comes from the government only
That is one source of secondary data.

q: What is secondary research?
r: Information that was already collected by others
Reports and articles are examples.
w: Information a business gathers itself for one purpose
That is primary research.
Information that is not useful to a business
Usefulness does not define it.
Information collected only through experiments
That is one primary method.

q: Which is an example of primary research?
r: Surveying customers about a new flavor
The business collects the data directly.
w: Reading an industry report published last year
That is secondary research.
Using census data from a government website
That is secondary research.
Reading a magazine article about trends
That is secondary research.

q: What is a survey?
r: A set of questions used to collect information from people
It can be done online, by phone or in person.
w: A tool that predicts next year's sales without any data
That is not a survey.
A report that lists a company's past expenses
That is a financial report.
A plan that decides where products will be placed
That is a distribution plan.

q: What is a focus group?
r: A small group that discusses a product or idea with a moderator
It gives in-depth opinions.
w: A large survey sent to thousands of anonymous customers
That is a survey.
A team of employees who set product prices
That is not a focus group.
A group of retailers that stock a product
That is not a focus group.

q: A company wants deep reasons why customers dislike its packaging. Which method fits best?
r: A focus group with open discussion
It reveals feelings and reasons.
w: A sales report listing total units sold last year
That does not explain reasons.
A price comparison against two competitors
That does not explain reasons.
A count of the stores that carry the product
That does not explain reasons.

q: What is a sample in marketing research?
r: A smaller group chosen to represent a larger population
Results are applied to the whole group.
w: A free product given out at a store event
That is a promotional sample.
A list of every customer a company has
That would be the whole population.
A draft of a new advertisement
That is a creative draft.

q: Why is a random sample useful?
r: Every member of the group has an equal chance of being chosen
It reduces bias.
w: It guarantees that everyone chosen will like the product
Opinions are not guaranteed.
It lets researchers choose only people they expect to agree
That would add bias.
It removes the need to ask any questions
Questions are still needed.

q: What is a database in marketing?
r: An organized collection of customer and market information
Marketers search it to find patterns.
w: A set of television commercials made for a brand
That is an ad library.
A building where products are stored before shipping
That is a warehouse.
A group of salespeople who call customers
That is a sales team.

q: What is customer relationship management (CRM) software used for?
r: Storing customer details and tracking interactions
It helps businesses serve customers better.
w: Printing price tags for the products in a store
That is a labeling task.
Scheduling delivery trucks for a distribution center
That is logistics software.
Designing the layout of a retail store
That is a design task.

q: A store notices that customers who buy a tent often buy sleeping bags too. How can it use this data?
r: Display the two items together and promote a bundle
Linked purchases suggest a useful offer.
w: Raise the price of tents so that fewer people buy them
That ignores the pattern.
Remove sleeping bags from the store entirely
That ignores the pattern.
Stop recording what customers buy at checkout
That removes useful data.

q: What is a demographic?
r: A characteristic of a population such as age, income or gender
Marketers use it to describe customers.
w: A type of advertisement shown on television
That is a media format.
A price that a company charges for a product
That is a price.
A store where a product is sold to buyers
That is a retailer.

q: What is psychographic information?
r: Data about customers' lifestyles, interests and attitudes
It describes why people buy.
w: Data about customers' ages and addresses only
That is demographic data.
Data about the prices of competing products
That is competitor data.
Data about the weather where customers live
That is geographic or environmental data.

q: Which is an example of psychographic data?
r: Customers who value eco-friendly products
It reflects attitudes and values.
w: Customers who are between 25 and 34 years old
That is demographic.
Customers who live in the same zip code
That is geographic.
Customers who earn over $50,000 a year
That is demographic.

q: What is market segmentation?
r: Dividing a market into groups with similar needs
It helps target the right customers.
w: Setting one price for every group of customers
That ignores differences.
Selling only to the largest customer in the market
That is not segmentation.
Combining all competitors into one group
That is not segmentation.

q: A sneaker company creates different ads for teens and for adults over 50. What is this?
r: Targeting market segments
Different groups receive different messages.
w: Mass marketing to a single large group
Different groups are being targeted.
Price fixing between two competing brands
That is an illegal practice.
Channel conflict between two retailers
That is not what the ads show.

q: What is data mining?
r: Searching large data sets for useful patterns
Businesses find trends they did not expect.
w: Digging for minerals used to make electronic parts
That is the physical industry.
Deleting old records to free up storage space
That is data cleanup.
Typing information into a spreadsheet by hand
That is data entry.

q: Why is data accuracy important in marketing?
r: Wrong data can lead to poor decisions
Decisions are only as good as the data.
w: Accurate data guarantees every campaign will succeed
No guarantee exists.
Accurate data removes the need for any research
Research is still needed.
Accurate data makes products cost less to produce
That is not the effect.

q: A survey was answered mostly by customers who already love the brand. What is the main problem?
r: Sample bias that may overstate satisfaction
The group does not represent all customers.
w: Too few questions on the printed form
The problem is who answered.
A price that is too high for customers
That is not the problem.
A store location that is too far away
That is not the problem.

q: What is a competitor analysis?
r: Studying rivals' products, prices and strategies
It helps a firm find its position.
w: Counting the employees who work for the firm
That is an internal count.
Reviewing a firm's own yearly tax filing
That is an accounting task.
Testing a firm's website speed
That is a technical test.

q: What is a SWOT analysis used for in marketing?
r: Reviewing strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
It guides planning.
w: Ranking customers by how much they spend each year
That is customer value analysis.
Counting the number of stores that sell a product
That is a distribution count.
Setting daily prices for products
That is a pricing task.

q: What is a trend?
r: A general direction in which something is changing
Marketers watch trends to spot opportunities.
w: A single sale made on one particular day
That is one event.
A fixed price that never changes
That is not a trend.
A product that is no longer sold
That is a discontinued item.

q: What is point-of-sale (POS) data?
r: Information collected when a sale is made
It shows what sold, when and for how much.
w: Information about a product's design
That is product data.
Information about a company's employees
That is HR data.
Information about a competitor's plans
That is competitive data.

q: POS data shows umbrella sales rising every time it rains. How should a store use this?
r: Stock more umbrellas when rain is forecast
Data guides inventory.
w: Reduce umbrella stock before rainy weeks
That ignores the pattern.
Raise the price of raincoats only in summer
That ignores the pattern.
Stop tracking weather and sales together
That removes useful insight.

q: What is customer privacy in marketing research?
r: Protecting personal information collected from customers
Companies should keep data safe.
w: Sharing customer data with every business that asks
That violates privacy.
Posting customers' names on a public board
That violates privacy.
Using data without telling customers how
That violates privacy.

q: A company wants to survey minors online. What should it consider first?
r: Laws that protect children's privacy and parental consent
Rules limit what can be collected.
w: Which prize will attract the most answers quickly
That ignores legal duties.
Whether the survey can be finished within a minute
That ignores legal duties.
Whether the questions are written in bold type
That ignores legal duties.

q: What is a marketing information system (MIS)?
r: A system that collects, organizes and reports marketing data
It supports decision making.
w: A system that delivers products to customers
That is a distribution system.
A system that prints advertisements for events
That is a print process.
A system that pays employees each month
That is payroll.

q: What is a questionnaire?
r: A written set of survey questions
Good questions are clear and unbiased.
w: A list of the answers a company wants to hear
That would add bias.
A report of final survey results
That is a results report.
A tool for printing coupons
That is a promotion tool.

q: Which survey question is the least biased?
r: How satisfied are you with our service?
It is neutral and open.
w: Don't you agree our amazing service is the best?
It pushes a particular answer.
Surely you loved our excellent service, right?
It pushes a particular answer.
Why is our service better than all others?
It pushes a particular answer.

q: What does a customer satisfaction score measure?
r: How happy customers are with a product or service
It is often collected through surveys.
w: How many customers visited a store last week
That is traffic.
How much a product costs to produce
That is cost.
How many ads were shown on television
That is reach.
